newsitem.title: USA: Problems will not derail space station, says NASA.
newsitem.headline: Problems will not derail space station, says NASA.

text.p: The international space station will remain on schedule despite Russian funding problems and the loss of two senior project officials, NASA's head of space flight said on Friday.
"We have had our share of problems," Wil Trafton told Reuters in an interview.
"I think when we're done, you'll find that the space station programme is in good health and we have essentially maintained the assembly sequence within a month or two."

Construction of the space station, which is led by NASA and includes contributions form Russia, Japan, Europe and Canada, was due to get underway in November, but a crucial Russian component is months behind schedule and threatens to upset the $40 billion project.
The Russian service module, which was to be the early control centre and living quarters for the station, was scheduled for launch in April 1998 but was running up to eight months behind schedule.

NASA decided in December to build an interim control module to perform some of the service module's tasks until it was in place. Trafton expected to select the design of the device by the end of January.
"We're looking at two vehicles," he said. "There's a Russian proposal on the table and there is a vehicle we're looking at in this country that has flown... before in a classified programme."

The interim control module would maintain the space station's orbital altitude for up to a year. The spacecraft would cost less than $100 million and could be paid for out of the project's reserve funds.

A more capable system, known as the propulsion module, also was being studied, but it would be difficult to pay for without breaking the space station's $2.1 billion a year spending limit, said Trafton.

Alexander Botvinko, deputy for human space flight at the Russian Space Agency, said the Russian parliament is expected to approve funds for the service module this month, which would lead to a launch by the end of 1998.

NASA officials were to travel to Moscow later this month to examine the extent of the service module problem. The issue also would be discussed when U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin meet in Washington in February.

Trafton said there was no connection between the space station's troubles and resignations this week of Andy Allen, an astronaut who helped manage the programme from NASA's Washington headquarters, and Dan Tam, the project's budget chief, who was based at the Johnson Space Centre in Houston.
"It's a coincidence," he said. "It is not a sign of bad things happening and I hope that it doesn't come across that way."
Allen said his decision to resign had nothing to do with station's problems and he was leaving the project confident it would succeed.
"It was just time to leave," he said. "I think the space station programme is real challenging. The Russians make it a little more challenging, but it is going to work"
Trafton also was upbeat about the project's future. He said NASA had helped its Canadian and European partners through budgetary difficulties and it was now Russia's turn.
"Nobody said this would be easy," he said. "This country has never attempted a programme of this nature before. But we come into it with a sense of optimism. We expect success -- not failure."
